title: Ezekiel 39:1–10
context: The LORD continues his message through Ezekiel against Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, begun in chapter 38. God will bring Gog from the far north onto the mountains of Israel, strike the weapons from his hands, and give his armies to the birds and animals; fire will fall on Magog and the coastlands, and the nations will know the LORD as the Holy One in Israel. Israel will burn the abandoned weapons as fuel for seven years and plunder those who plundered them. Gog, Magog, and the word rendered Rosh, and how this prophecy relates to Revelation 20:8, are discussed at 38:1–9; the same range of readings is in view here.

verses.text: “You, son of man, prophesy against Gog, and say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, “prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal.” The oracle of chapter 38 continues.

Arminian readers see God opposing a power that sets itself against his restored people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Meshech and Tubal appear among Japheth’s sons in Genesis 10:2. Readers identify Rosh and Gog himself in different ways, and Gog’s identity remains uncertain.

Reformed readers see God ruling over hostile nations. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I will turn you around, will lead you on, and will cause you to come up from the uttermost parts of the north; and I will bring you onto the mountains of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will turn Gog around, lead him on, and bring him from the far north onto the mountains of Israel. God directs the invader’s course.

Arminian readers see God steering a power already bent on aggression.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse echoes 38:4 and 38:16, where God also brings Gog against the land.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over the movements of nations. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s rule over hostile powers, without settling how his direction relates to Gog’s own intent. See the Judges 9:23 box, as at 38:4.

verses.text: I will strike your bow out of your left hand, and will cause your arrows to fall out of your right hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will strike the bow from Gog’s left hand and make the arrows fall from his right. The invader is disarmed.

Arminian readers see human military strength rendered useless before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image pictures defeat by God’s action rather than by Israel’s army.

Reformed readers see deliverance as God’s work alone. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s power to protect his people when their own strength is not the decisive factor.

verses.text: You will fall on the mountains of Israel, you, and all your hordes, and the peoples who are with you. I will give you to the ravenous birds of every sort and to the animals of the field to be devoured.
verses.arminianNotes:
Gog, his hordes, and the peoples with him will fall on the mountains of Israel and be given to birds and animals. Defeat is total.

Arminian readers see judgment on aggression against God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes:
To be left unburied was a sign of utter disgrace in the ancient world; the image anticipates 39:17–20.

Reformed readers see God’s justice against those who oppose him. Both traditions read this as shared ground and handle the image soberly.

verses.text: You will fall on the open field, for I have spoken it,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Gog will fall in the open field, for the Lord GOD has spoken. The word guarantees the outcome.

Arminian readers see the certainty of judgment once God has announced it against a persistent aggressor.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase “for I have spoken it” grounds the outcome in God’s word.

Reformed readers see God’s word as effective and sure. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reliability of what God declares, whatever readers conclude about when and how the prophecy is fulfilled.

verses.text: “I will send a fire on Magog and on those who dwell securely in the islands. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will send fire on Magog and on those living securely in the islands, and they will know he is the LORD. Judgment reaches Gog’s homeland.

Arminian readers see God’s justice reaching beyond the battlefield.
verses.reformedNotes:
The location of Magog is uncertain; 38:2 calls Gog “of the land of Magog.” The islands may refer to distant coastlands.

Reformed readers see God’s rule over distant lands. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘ “I will make my holy name known among my people Israel. I won’t allow my holy name to be profaned any more. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, the Holy One in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will make his holy name known among Israel and no longer allow it to be profaned; the nations will know he is “the Holy One in Israel.” God’s name is the concern.

Arminian readers see God acting so all may know him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Concern for God’s holy name runs through Ezekiel (compare 36:22–23).

Reformed readers see God acting for his own glory. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God vindicating his name before Israel and the nations.

verses.text: Behold, it comes, and it will be done,” says the Lord GOD. “This is the day about which I have spoken.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says, “Behold, it comes, and it will be done,” calling it the day of which he has spoken. The event is certain.

Arminian readers see God’s announced purposes coming to pass.
verses.reformedNotes:
The reference to a day spoken of before may echo 38:17, which asks whether Gog is the one spoken of by earlier prophets. Readers differ on the timing and referent.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose sure. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Those who dwell in the cities of Israel will go out and will make fires of the weapons and burn them, both the shields and the bucklers, the bows and the arrows, and the war clubs and the spears, and they will make fires with them for seven years;
verses.arminianNotes:
Those in Israel’s cities will burn Gog’s weapons, shields, bows, arrows, clubs, and spears, as fuel for seven years. The weapons of war become firewood.

Arminian readers see peace replacing the threat of war.
verses.reformedNotes:
The seven years may signal completeness or the vastness of the defeated army; readers differ on whether the number is literal or symbolic.

Reformed readers see God turning instruments of war to peaceful use. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: so that they will take no wood out of the field, and not cut down any out of the forests; for they will make fires with the weapons. They will plunder those who plundered them, and rob those who robbed them,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
They will take no wood from field or forest, for the weapons will be their fuel, and they will plunder those who plundered them. The tables are turned.

Arminian readers see justice restoring what aggressors took.
verses.reformedNotes:
The reversal echoes 38:12–13, where Gog came to take plunder. The fuel detail may be pictorial rather than a practical forecast; readers differ.

Reformed readers see God reversing the fortunes of his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
